title: what karma actually keeps track of
hook: instant karma, the comments say; the word is older, and it points at you

segments.voice: Yesterday: the shadow, and what bugs me may be mine. Six words so far: meant to be, breathe, memento mori, namaste, manifesting, the shadow. Today, the seventh.
screen: `MEANT TO BE · BREATHE · MEMENTO MORI · NAMASTE · MANIFESTING · THE SHADOW`

segments.voice: Karma. The ex who cheated gets a flat tire. Someone cuts the line and spills their coffee. Instant karma, the comments say. Used like that, it's the universe keeping score and paying out where you can watch. It's a satisfying idea. The word is far older than that use, and it points the other way: not at them. At you.
screen: `KARMA.` → `THE FLAT TIRE. THE SPILLED COFFEE.` → `PAYBACK?` → `NOT QUITE.`

segments.voice: Karma is Sanskrit for action. A deed. Hindu, Buddhist, Jain and Sikh teachers all use the word, and they don't all use it the same way. Many teach that what we do shapes what comes after, in this life and, as a matter of faith, in lives to come. The Buddha made a sharp move. Intention, he told his monks, is what I call karma. Not only what your hands did: what you meant by it. The choice is the seed. Then a surprise. He listed the exact workings of karma among a few things not worth trying to figure out, because chasing them only leads to frustration. So the version that keeps score on other people, did they get what's coming, is the one the old teachers spent the least time on. The older word turns you around. Not, what will happen to them? But, what am I planting with this choice, right now? It's the one piece you can actually see, and the one piece that's yours.
screen: `KARMA — ACTION, A DEED.` · `INTENTION IS WHAT I CALL KARMA.` · `DON'T TRY TO CALCULATE IT.` · `WHAT AM I PLANTING?`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, bring to mind one choice you'll make today: a reply, a tone of voice, a small favor. On the second, notice the intention underneath it. On the third, choose the seed you'd like it to be.
Karma. Action, and the intention inside it. Not a scoreboard. Seventh word: a week's worth.
Your line: the intention is the seed. That's week one: seven words people borrow every day, and what's actually inside them. Tomorrow, the thoughts that aren't you.

screen: `DAY 7 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE THOUGHTS THAT AREN'T YOU.`

howItsDone: Hindu, Buddhist, Jain and Sikh traditions all teach about karma in their own ways; many Buddhists reflect on their intentions before acting, and many Hindus speak of karma as action and its fruit, in this life and across lifetimes.

original.note: Sanskrit: action, deed. In Pali, the language of early Buddhist texts, it's kamma.

trapdoor: what you thought: payback. the universe keeping score.
what it means: action, and the intention inside it.
what a scholar hears: Anguttara Nikaya 6.63, cetanāhaṃ kammaṃ vadāmi, intention, monks, is what I call kamma; AN 4.77 lists the results of kamma among four imponderables.

story.title: the bandit who stopped
story.text: A bandit who wears a necklace of his victims' fingers sees a lone monk on the road and runs to kill him. However fast he runs, he can't catch the monk, who is only walking. Stop, he shouts. I have stopped, the monk says. You stop too. The bandit throws down his sword and becomes a monk himself. Later, people throw stones at him in the street, and his teacher tells him to bear it: he's living out the fruit of what he once did.
story.source: early Buddhist texts: Majjhima Nikaya 86 (Angulimala Sutta)
